opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that every major leap we've seen in AI so far has come from finding a way to scale data, not just from clever architecture. Language models got where they are because the internet had already accumulated trillions of tokens of human text for us. Vision had ImageNet, then web-scale image-text pairs. In embodied intelligence, we simply don't have that. There's no "internet of robot actions" sitting around waiting to be crawled.

So right now, a lot of embodied work borrows heavily from language and vision models, which makes sense as a starting point, since they bring world knowledge, semantics, and some common sense. But a model that only understands the world through text and pictures doesn't really understand physical interaction: how much force to apply, what happens when you push something, how objects deform or slip. That kind of knowledge lives in action data, in the closed loop between perception and control. If embodied intelligence is always just a thin adapter on top of a language model, it will never have its own foundation. It'll be a borrowed brain with clumsy hands.

For embodied AI to develop its own model, something native to the physical world, it needs its own data flywheel at a scale comparable to what language had. And that's hard, because real-world robot data is expensive, slow to collect, and hardware-dependent. That's why I think the question of how to scale data is really the central question of the field right now. Whether it's through large-scale teleoperation, human video, simulation, or generative world models that can synthesize realistic interactions, the field has to solve the data problem first. Model design matters, of course, but historically, once data scales, the right architectures tend to emerge. Without the data, even the best architecture has nothing to learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied AI needs its own physical-world data flywheel at scale to develop a native foundation model, and identifies scaling data as central to that goal.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll draft the guest response now.

I think the clearest lesson from the last few years in AI is that the model is really the shadow of the data. Look at what happened with language and with vision. Nobody hand-designed GPT's understanding of grammar or reasoning. It emerged because the model saw an enormous, diverse corpus of text. Same with image generation. The architectures mattered, but they were almost secondary. What changed everything was the scale and diversity of what the model was trained on.

Now bring that to embodied intelligence. Today most robotics work still runs on a few hundred or a few thousand demonstrations collected in one lab, on one robot, in one room. You can get a nice demo out of that. But it doesn't generalize. Move the cup two centimeters, change the lighting, swap the gripper, and it falls apart. That's not a failure of the algorithm, it's a failure of coverage. The model has simply never seen enough of the world to form a general notion of what manipulation is.

So when I say data scaling is crucial for embodied intelligence to have its own foundation model, I mean something specific. Language models borrow their world knowledge from text written by humans. Robots can't borrow in the same way, because the physical world doesn't come pre-tokenized. Contact, friction, deformable objects, the feel of a grasp, these things don't exist on the internet in a usable form. We have to generate that data ourselves. That's the bottleneck, and it's a very different kind of bottleneck than language faced.

And there's a second reason. In language, we got the scaling laws almost for free, because the data was already there and we just kept adding compute. In robotics we don't yet know what the scaling curve looks like, because no one has had enough data to draw it. My bet is that the curve exists, and that once we pass some threshold of diverse, real-world interaction data, we'll see the same kind of emergent generalization we saw with text. But you can't discover that threshold by thinking about it. You have to collect your way there.

So that's why I'm so focused on the data side. The question isn't whether a transformer can control a robot. It clearly can. The question is whether we can build the pipeline, real robot data, teleoperation, simulation, video from humans, all of it combined, at a scale that lets the model actually learn the physics of the world instead of memorizing one lab. Whoever solves that gets the foundation model for embodiment. The architecture will follow.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly connects scaling data to embodied intelligence developing its own foundation model, explaining that broad interaction data is needed for the model to learn physical-world behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that embodied intelligence has to learn through interaction. A model needs to understand not only what it sees, but what will happen when it takes an action, and how to adjust when the outcome is different from what it expected.

That requires a lot of diverse experience. If a robot only learns one task in one environment, it can easily learn something very specific to that setup. Change the object, the lighting, or the position, and it may struggle. By scaling up data across tasks, environments, and interactions, we give the model a chance to learn patterns that generalize.

So it’s not just about collecting more images or videos. We need data that connects observations, actions, and outcomes. Models trained on language and vision give us a useful starting point, but embodied intelligence needs that additional experience of acting in the world to develop its own capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied intelligence needs interaction data to develop its own capabilities, but does not clearly connect scaling data to developing a dedicated model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that embodied intelligence has to learn from interaction. A model needs to understand not only what it sees, but what will happen when it takes an action—and how to adjust when the result is different from what it expected.

That requires a lot of diverse experience. If a robot only practices one task in one environment, it can learn a very narrow solution. Change the object, the lighting, or the layout, and that solution may fail. Scaling up data gives it the opportunity to learn patterns that transfer across those variations.

But scale isn’t just about collecting more hours. The data needs to connect observations, actions, and outcomes, and cover different tasks and environments. That’s what could allow us to move from building a separate system for each task toward a general model that can adapt to new situations.

r001.rationale: The response explains how more diverse interaction data could support a general, adaptable model, but does not say that scaling data matters because embodied intelligence is expected to develop its own dedicated model.
